pr.title: coverage: Eliminate more counters by giving them to unreachable nodes
pr.description:
When preparing a function's coverage counters and metadata during codegen, any part of the original coverage graph that was removed by MIR optimizations can be treated as having an execution count of zero.

Somewhat counter-intuitively, if we give those unreachable nodes a _higher_ priority for receiving physical counters (instead of counter expressions), that ends up reducing the total number of physical counters needed.

This works because if a node is unreachable, we don't actually create a physical counter for it. Instead that node gets a fixed zero counter, and any other node that would have relied on that physical counter in its counter expression can just ignore that term completely.
pr.author: Zalathar

processing.reason: This PR is a coverage-metadata optimization, not a semantics-changing MIR rewrite. It reorders the coverage `priority_list` and removes `pos`/`neg` sorts so that MIR-eliminated (unreachable) BCBs receive fixed `Zero` counters, reducing the highest physical counter ID in `.cov-map` goldens (e.g. `assert_not::main` c3→c0). The actual Rust program's runtime behavior and return values are unchanged; only instrumented coverage counter allocation/metadata differs. As the supplied test strategy itself states, “Do not treat the `.cov-map` churn as program-output changes; these are coverage metadata/counter-ID differences.” Therefore no source-grounded pair of Rust functions with the same signature/inputs can exhibit different defined runtime values for the pre-patch versus post-patch transformation. Encoding the priority-list sort as a standalone algorithm and comparing counter IDs would only model coverage metadata, not the required original/transformed program semantics, and would not be a valid compiler-regression counterexample.

analysis.originalLogic: During coverage codegen, `coverage_ids_info` built `priority_list` from the function's coverage graph, kept the synthetic sink first, and passed the list unchanged to `make_node_counters`. `transcribe_counters` then converted node counters into physical counters/expressions, and additionally sorted the `pos` and `neg` operand lists before constructing the final counter expression.
analysis.incorrectTransformation: The historical behavior left `priority_list[1..]` in its original order, so nodes removed by MIR optimizations (unreachable nodes not present in `bcbs_seen`) were not deliberately partitioned later in the priority list. `transcribe_counters` also sorted its `pos`/`neg` operand lists even though that sorting was no longer needed. This failed to exploit the fact that MIR-eliminated nodes can receive fixed zero counters: expressions could continue to retain physical-counter dependencies on such nodes instead of dropping those terms, leaving more physical counters in the coverage mapping.
analysis.inputDomain: Rust functions compiled with coverage instrumentation (`-C instrument-coverage`) whose original coverage graph contains basic coverage blocks that MIR optimizations remove, e.g. trivial `assert!`/`assert_not!`-style branches, `while` loops, drop glue, async closures, generic wrappers, and condition-heavy control flow. The relevant input dimension is whether a BCB from the pre-optimization coverage graph is absent from `bcbs_seen` because MIR opts made it unreachable.
analysis.summary: InstrumentCoverage can reduce physical counter allocation by keeping the synthetic sink first and re-partitioning the rest of the priority list so MIR-eliminated (unreachable) nodes are later and thus more likely to receive physical counter slots. Those slots are then replaced by fixed Zero counters, and expressions can omit the corresponding terms, reducing total physical counters. The patch also removes now-unnecessary `pos`/`neg` sorts in `transcribe_counters`; golden `.cov-map` tests show reduced highest counter IDs.
analysis.trigger: A function has coverage BCBs that were removed by MIR optimizations, especially when those unreachable nodes would otherwise occupy priority-list positions that affect physical-counter assignment. Trigger by compiling instrumented code containing branches/loops/assertions that MIR optimizations can prove unreachable or eliminate.
preconditions: Coverage instrumentation and coverage counter/metadata preparation are enabled for the function.
The original coverage graph contains nodes that were removed by MIR optimizations, so they are not in `bcbs_seen`.
The synthetic sink node remains the first element of the priority list and must never receive a physical counter.
The reachable/unreachable partition is applied only to `priority_list[1..]`; the original relative ordering is preserved within each partition.
pitfalls: Do not re-sort the entire priority list: `priority_list[0]` is the synthetic sink and must remain first so it never gets a physical counter.

Do not conclude that giving unreachable nodes lower priority reduces counters; the patch intentionally sorts them later because that makes them more likely to receive physical counter slots, which are then converted to fixed zero counters.
Do not retain the old `pos.sort()`/`neg.sort()` calls in `transcribe_counters` after adding the partition; the patch removes them as unnecessary.
Do not expect the transformation to simply delete unreachable mappings: `assert_not.cov-map` still contains the relevant mappings, but they use `Code(Counter(0))`/zero rather than extra counters.
Do not treat the `.cov-map` churn as program-output changes; these are coverage metadata/counter-ID differences.
analysis.testStrategy: Use coverage golden tests (`tests/coverage/*.cov-map`) and compare counter assignments before/after the transformation. Focus on functions with MIR-removed unreachable nodes, such as the `assert_not`, `while`, `drop_trait`, `generics`, `async2`, `conditions`, and `try_error_result` cases in the patch. Build paired inputs that differ only in whether a branch/assertion is provably unreachable/MIR-eliminated, then verify the instrumented coverage map uses fixed Zero/omitted terms and a lower highest counter ID (for example, the patch changes `assert_not::main` from `Highest counter ID seen: c3` to `Highest counter ID seen: c0`). Also verify the sink remains first and does not receive a physical counter. No compiler execution or reproduction is claimed here; these are source/test-diff-derived checks.
evidence: When preparing a function's coverage counters and metadata during codegen, any part of the original coverage graph that was removed by MIR optimizations can be treated as having an execution count of zero.

Somewhat counter-intuitively, if we give those unreachable nodes a _higher_ priority for receiving physical counters (instead of counter expressions), that ends up reducing the total number of physical counters needed.

This works because if a node is unreachable, we don't actually create a physical counter for it. Instead that node gets a fixed zero counter, and any other node that would have relied on that physical counter in its counter expression can just ignore that term completely.
